segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus was led up into the wilderness by the Spirit, to be tested by the devil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterward he was hungry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The tester came up and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become loaves of bread.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is written: ‘A person will not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes out through the mouth of God.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written: ‘He will give his angels orders concerning you, and on their hands they will lift you up, so that you never strike your foot against a stone.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Again, it is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go away, Satan! For it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the devil left him, and look, angels came and began to wait on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Leaving Nazareth, he went and settled in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations—

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: the people sitting in darkness saw a great light, and on those sitting in the region and shadow of death a light dawned.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From then on Jesus began to proclaim and say,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Repent, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once they left their nets and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, putting their nets in order, and he called them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once they left the boat and their father and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went around all of Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity among the people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The report about him spread into all Syria, and they brought him all who were ill, those gripped by various diseases and torments, the demon-possessed, those having seizures, and the paralyzed, and he healed them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Large crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.

notes.note: The Greek verb means to put someone to the test, whether to prove them or to make them fail; English ‘tempt’ has narrowed to enticement. ‘Tested’ keeps the link with Israel's forty years of testing in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2) and with Jesus's reply in verse 7, which uses a compound of the same verb. Most translations keep ‘tempted’ and ‘the tempter’ because the devil's intent is hostile; that hostile sense is within the range of the Greek word.

All three of Jesus's replies quote Deuteronomy (8:3, 6:16, 6:13), from Moses' review of Israel's testing in the wilderness. A reader who knew the Scriptures would see Jesus, just named God's Son, reliving Israel's wilderness trial and passing it. The devil's quotation in verse 6 is from Psalm 91:11–12.

The Greek word means a little wing, and so a projecting tip or edge. Which part of the temple complex is meant is unknown; suggestions include a corner of the outer colonnade high above the Kidron valley and a point on the roof of the sanctuary itself. The traditional word is kept because nothing more precise can be justified.

The verb denotes bowing or prostrating oneself before a superior, a gesture offered to kings as well as to gods. The scriptural reply in verse 10 shows that the homage demanded here is the kind owed to God alone, so ‘worship’ is retained.

The verb's ordinary sense is attending to someone's needs, especially serving food at table. After a forty-day fast the likely meaning is that the angels brought him food, though the word can cover care more broadly. ‘Ministered’ now suggests religious activity that the Greek does not imply.

The Greek says only that John was handed over, without saying by whom or to whom; the reference is to his imprisonment by Herod Antipas. Matthew later uses the same verb repeatedly for what is done to Jesus, and the literal rendering keeps that echo audible.

The Greek word is the ordinary plural ‘nations’ or ‘peoples’, used in Jewish Greek for the non-Jewish peoples; ‘Gentiles’ is a Latin-derived term that hides this. The quotation is from Isaiah 9:1–2, where the northern tribal lands, the first to fall to Assyria, are promised light. Matthew's wording differs in places from both the Hebrew and the Septuagint.

The Greek is plural, reflecting the Hebrew and Aramaic word for heaven, which is always plural in form. The phrase is found only in Matthew in the New Testament; most scholars take it as equivalent to ‘the kingdom of God’ in the other Gospels, though some think Matthew intends a contrast between heaven and earth.

The Greek word is the general term for human beings, not the word for males. ‘Fishers’ is used in both verses 18 and 19 because the Greek repeats the same noun, and the saying depends on the repetition.

The Greek word means literally ‘moonstruck’ and names a condition of recurring seizures that ancient people associated with the phases of the moon. Many translations use ‘epileptics’, which may well be the condition in view; the rendering here describes the symptoms without importing a modern diagnosis.

candidates.reason: Translators split between ‘tempt’ and ‘test’ across the Gospels, James, Hebrews and the Lord's Prayer noun πειρασμός, and readers lose the links if the English varies.
The verb covers prostration before humans and worship of God; whether to render ‘worship’, ‘bow down’ or ‘pay homage’ needs a consistent rule, especially where Jesus is the object.
The plural is rendered ‘Gentiles’, ‘nations’ or ‘pagans’ by different translators, and the choice affects Paul's letters and Acts throughout.
‘Repent’ may suggest remorse or penance to modern readers, whereas the Greek centres on a change of mind and direction; the verb and its noun recur across the whole New Testament.
It is rendered ‘betray’, ‘arrest’, ‘deliver up’ and ‘hand over’ in different places, which obscures the deliberate echo between John, Jesus and the disciples.
